title: Fixed project or ongoing partnership
excerpt: Choose a fixed project when the launch has an edge you can describe. Choose an ongoing partnership when the product keeps changing and you want the same people on it.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The corridor suggests a place you keep returning to, which is the feeling of an ongoing partnership.
caption: Some work ends at a door. Some keeps a room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is a fixed project the right contract?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed project when you can name the edge: the pages or the workflow, the action the work should earn, and what done looks like. A marketing site, a catalog rebuild, or a first product slice with empty and error states are typical. The date and the price depend on that edge staying still.

faqs.question: When is an ongoing partnership the right contract?
faqs.answer: Use an ongoing partnership when the product or the site will keep changing and you want the same people to change it. The work has a cadence and a priority list, not a single launch line. You still own the repository, the domain, and the content. The partnership is time and judgment, not custody of your company.

faqs.question: Can a fixed project become an ongoing partnership?
faqs.answer: Yes, after the launch has shown what kind of change is real. Start the next agreement from that evidence: what you edit every week, what broke, what you postponed. Do not convert a project into a retainer halfway through in order to absorb an undefined idea. Finish the edge, then decide.

markdown:
The design retainer vs project decision is about whether the work has an edge. Choose a fixed project for a launch you can describe. Choose an ongoing partnership when the product keeps changing and you want the same people to change it with you.

Both can be honest. They fail in different ways. A fixed project fails when the edge was never real and every week adds a page. An ongoing partnership fails when nobody sets priorities, and the month becomes a stream of small favors. Pick the shape that matches the work, then hold it.

## A fixed project for a launch with an edge

A fixed project has a finish line both sides can point at. A marketing site with a known set of pages. A shop migration that brings the catalog, the URLs, and a checkout that works. A product slice with one workflow, including the empty state and the error. When that line is crossed, the project is over, whether or not your company is.

The price and the date mean something because the edge is written down. What is in. What is out. What a change does to the date. You are buying a result, not a block of hours that can be reinterpreted as a different product.

This is the right shape for a first serious site, a redesign with a season attached, or a brand system small enough to hand over. Hanabi’s studio work often looks like this: design and production code, a repository you own, and a portal for the files and updates that should outlast the project. Done includes the handoff, not only the URL.

A fixed project is the wrong container for “we will figure out the product as we go” unless the thing you are figuring out is explicitly a first slice, priced as a slice. Call that a fixed project too, with a smaller edge. Do not call the entire unknown a fixed project and hope the invoice survives contact with reality.

At the end, you should be able to run the thing without the studio in the room. You have the repo, the domain, the content logins, and a note on how to publish. You may still want help next month. You should not be stuck.

## An ongoing partnership when the same people should stay

An ongoing partnership is for change that does not stop at launch. The product grows a second workflow. The shop adds a season and the grid has to stay consistent. The site needs a page when the offer shifts, and you want the type, the code, and the judgment to match what already shipped.

You are buying continuity. The people who made the decisions are the people who extend them. That is worth it when restarting with a new team would mean re-explaining the brand, the repository, and the refusals. It is not worth it when the remaining work is a narrow skill once a quarter. A freelancer or an in-house hire may fit that rhythm better.

The partnership still needs an edge, just a shorter one. A month has a priority: these fixes, this page, this state. Unprioritized access becomes a chat channel with no project inside it. Write the priority. Review it on a cadence. Park the rest.

Ownership does not flip because the relationship continues. The repository, the domain, the analytics, and the content stay in your accounts. A retainer that also holds the only admin login is a dependency with a monthly bill. Hanabi’s version of staying after delivery is the portal and the codebase you can open, plus people who can keep working in them. The company remains yours.

Speed remains a public fact, not a feeling. Google’s [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are the useful targets: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, cumulative layout shift under 0.1. A fixed project should meet that bar at launch. An ongoing partnership should keep meeting it as images, scripts, and pages accumulate. Put a check in the cadence. A month that only adds weight is a month that spent the brand’s clarity.

## What changes in the week

The week looks different, and you should feel the difference.

On a fixed project, the week is aimed at the edge. Reviews compare the work to the brief. New ideas are written down and, unless they replace something, they wait. The timeline is a date with assumptions: copy by Thursday, review on Monday. Communication is there so the date stays honest.

On an ongoing partnership, the week is aimed at the top of the list. There may be no single launch. There is still a demo of what changed, a note on what is next, and a decision about what will not be touched. Flexibility is the point, and it still needs a written trade so the month does not fill with half-finished experiments.

Money follows the same split. A fixed project is priced against the edge, with change handled as change. An ongoing partnership is priced against capacity: a known amount of design and build, used on the priorities you set. Spending it on emergencies every week means the priorities were wishes. Say so in the review, and reset the list.

Neither shape is a discount on thinking. The studio still decides what is clear, what is on brand, and what should ship. You still decide the offer and the approver. A retainer does not mean the team will implement every sketch. A fixed project does not mean they will refuse to hear that the goal was wrong. It means the hearing has a consequence you both accept.

## What you still decide up front

Choose using two questions.

Does the work have a finish line you can describe without using the phrase “and so on”? If yes, start with a fixed project. If the honest description is “the product will keep moving and we want this team on it,” start with an ongoing partnership, and still name the first month’s list.

Do you need design and build together the whole time? If the next stretch is only illustration, or only a campaign, you may not need the studio’s full shape. If every change touches the interface and the code, continuity is the product you are buying.

Say the review rule before you sign. Who approves. How fast a decision comes back. What happens to a request that arrives outside the list. Those habits matter more under a retainer, because there is no final invoice to force a cleanup. They matter on a fixed project because the date is the cleanup.

Also say how you will stop. A fixed project stops at the edge, with a handoff. An ongoing partnership should stop cleanly too: notice, a last list, access remains yours, files are in the portal or the repo. A relationship that cannot end is not a partnership. It is a lock-in.

## How to switch shapes

Start fixed when you are unsure. A first slice will teach you whether the work keeps going. At the end, look at what you postponed and what you edited twice. If the list is alive, talk about an ongoing partnership with that list as month one. If the list is empty, stop. You have the site.

Switch the other way with the same honesty. An ongoing partnership that has drifted into “one more launch” with a hard date may need a fixed project beside it, with an edge, so the date is not eaten by the queue. Name the launch as its own scope. Let the monthly work pause or shrink so the edge can be real.

Do not use a retainer to avoid scoping, and do not use a fixed price to avoid a conversation about what happens after launch. The shape is there to make the next month understandable.

The choice sits next to a wider one: whether you need a studio at all, or a freelancer, or someone in-house. That piece is [studio, freelancer, or in-house for a first serious site](/blog/studio-freelancer-or-in-house).

If you are deciding which shape fits a real launch, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the edge if you have one, or the list of what keeps changing. The call should end with the contract shape, not a vague agreement to “start and see.”
